title: The letters of John
tagline: A letter from an eyewitness about light, love and belief, and two short notes from “the elder” about truth and hospitality.

intro.text: Three letters have long been linked with John. The first gives no name and reads like a sermon; the second and third are brief notes from someone who calls himself only “the elder”. Early tradition places all three at Ephesus near the end of the first century.

They were written to people unsettled by a split. Some had left (“they went out from us”) and denied that Jesus Christ had come in the flesh; the writer answers with tests anyone can apply: doing what is right, loving one another, and believing in Jesus as the Christ.

2 and 3 John are the two shortest books of the New Testament. By verses 2 John is shortest, with 13; by words 3 John is, with 294 words in the King James and 219 in the Greek, against 298 and 249 for 2 John. Origen remarked that the two together “do not contain hundred lines”.

author.text: The letter never names its writer. He speaks as an eyewitness of “the Word of life”, one who has heard, seen and handled it, and he writes with a teacher's warmth to “my little children”. From the second century the letter was read as the work of John, “the disciple of the Lord”; who wrote it is discussed below.

recipients.text: No one is named. Westcott and Plummer think it went first to the circle of churches in the province of Asia around Ephesus; Brooke thinks it was almost certainly written for a definite church or group of churches. Plummer notes that the absence of Old Testament quotations and the closing warning against idols suggest readers who had come to faith from paganism.

writtenFrom.text: Ephesus, by early tradition. Irenaeus says John lived at Ephesus until the time of Trajan, and Eusebius repeats the tradition that he settled there after his exile. Brooke speaks of a universal tradition linking the letters with Ephesus, or at least Asia Minor.

date.text: Disputed. Westcott places it in the last decade of the first century, Plummer about AD 85–95, and Smith at the close of the century; Brooke says it cannot be later than about AD 110, because Papias and Polycarp already knew it. An older reading of “it is the last time” as the eve of Jerusalem's fall would put it before AD 70; Plummer records that reading and rejects it. Whether the letter came before or after John's Gospel is also unsettled: Lightfoot thought they were sent together, most scholars put the letter later, and Westcott found no sure way to tell.

occasion.text: A group had broken away: “they went out from us, but they were not of us.” They denied that Jesus is the Christ and would not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. The writer calls them “many antichrists” and “false prophets”, and writes to steady those who remained.

themes.text: God is light, so walking in the light means owning up to sin and keeping his commandments.
God is love. Love begins with God, not with us: “not that we loved God, but that he loved us.”
The incarnation is real. The life “was manifested”, seen and handled, and Jesus Christ “is come in the flesh”.

Sin and forgiveness: confession and cleansing, Christ the advocate with the Father, and Christ the propitiation for sins. The Greek word for propitiation, hilasmos, occurs in the New Testament only in these two verses of 1 John.

The tests of life. Robert Law reads the letter as a set of tests by which readers can know they are “begotten of God”: doing what is right, loving one another, and believing that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh. Each test is run three times, at a higher level each time. Law divides verses 3:10 and 3:24 in the middle; the outline here places each divided verse with the earlier part.

“Hereby we know.” Nine verses in the King James Version give a way of knowing (“hereby we do know that we know him”, “hereby know ye the Spirit of God”…), and the letter ends with a threefold “we know”.
Claims put to the test. “If we say…” and “He that saith…” introduce claims the writer weighs against conduct; Law suggests they may echo the opponents' own slogans.
Abiding. The verb menō, “abide, dwell, remain”, comes 23 times in the Greek: abiding in God, in the Son, in the light, and God's word abiding in his people.
Children of God and children of the devil are told apart by what they do.
The world is passing away, and faith overcomes it: “this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith.” That is the only use of the noun “faith” in the three letters.
Assurance: the letter says it was written “that ye may know that ye have eternal life”. Westcott sets this beside the purpose of John's Gospel and finds the two in full harmony.

No Old Testament quotation. 1 John quotes no Old Testament passage. Its one clear allusion is to Cain, who “slew his brother” (Genesis 4:8); Law calls Cain the prototype of hate, set against Christ who laid down his life for us. Cain is the only person named in the letter besides Jesus Christ.

Words that are only here. “Antichrist” appears in the Bible only in 1 and 2 John, five times in all. Paraklētos, “advocate” in 1 John 2:1, is the word John's Gospel uses for the “Comforter”, and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament.

keyVerses.why: “God is light”: the thesis of the letter's first half in Plummer's outline.
The test of honesty about sin, and the promise of forgiveness.
Love tested from the other side: “Love not the world”.
Being called God's children, the subject of the second cycle.
Love defined by the cross: “he laid down his life for us”.
Where love comes from: “because he first loved us”.
The letter's own statement of its purpose.

outline.title: Prologue: the Word of life we saw and touched
First cycle · walking in the light: obedience
First cycle · the old and new commandment: love
First cycle · the antichrists and the anointing: belief
Second cycle · God's children do what is right
Second cycle · love in deed and in truth
Second cycle · test the spirits: belief
Third cycle · the faith that overcomes, and God's witness

words.note: The King James tags show 29, because one Greek word is sometimes tagged on two English words.
Tischendorf's Greek text has 6: at 2:7 it reads “Beloved” where the King James has “Brethren”.
Counted in the sense “know” only. Strong's files some forms of “see” and “behold” under the same number, so the King James tags show 17.
Tischendorf's Greek text has one more, at 4:16.
One of the seven is in the “three heavenly witnesses” words of 5:7–8, so Tischendorf's text has 6.
The Greek text behind the King James has a longer 5:13, which adds one; Tischendorf's text has 9.
Found in the Bible only in 1 and 2 John.

people.name: Cain
people.note: “Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother.” An allusion to Genesis 4:8, and the only Old Testament figure in the letter. In the New Testament Cain is named only here, in Hebrews 11:4 and in Jude 11.

places.name: Ephesus
places.note: Not named in the letter. Early tradition places John at Ephesus late in his life.

author.text: The writer calls himself only “the elder” (Greek ho presbyteros). Whether this elder is the apostle John or another John is discussed below. The letter repeats the teaching of 1 John so closely that Easton counts seven of its thirteen verses as already found in the first letter.

recipients.text: “The elect lady and her children.” Whether she is a woman or a church, personified, is an old question (see below). The letter closes with greetings from “the children of thy elect sister”.

writtenFrom.text: Probably Ephesus, like 1 John: Plummer, Westcott and Easton think the short letters were written from the same place, soon after the first.

date.text: Disputed with 1 John. Plummer, Westcott and Easton place it soon after the first letter, since it assumes that letter's teaching and shares formulas with 3 John.

occasion.text: Travelling teachers depended on the hospitality of local Christians, and some of them were “deceivers” who did not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. The elder rejoices that her children walk in truth, repeats the command to love, and asks that such teachers be given neither welcome nor greeting. Brooke sees advice about receiving visitors as the letter's chief object.

themes.text: Truth and love held together: “in truth and love”.
Love means keeping the commandment the readers have had “from the beginning”.
Abiding in “the doctrine of Christ” is how one has both the Father and the Son.
Careful hospitality: a teacher who brings another doctrine is not to be received or greeted.
Truth is the signature word. It comes five times in 2 John, about 20 times per thousand Greek words, against about 4 in 1 John; Law calls truth the keynote of the letter.

A small difference in the Greek at verse 7: the text behind the King James reads that the deceivers “are entered into” the world, while Tischendorf and Westcott read that they “are gone forth” into it.

A slow road into the canon. Eusebius listed 2 and 3 John among the disputed books, and the Syriac churches' Peshitta translation does not include them; Westcott puts this down to their small circulation and to the bare title “the elder”.

keyVerses.why: Grace, mercy and peace “in truth and love”: the letter's two words together.
“This is love, that we walk after his commandments.”
The deceivers who do not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.
Abiding in the doctrine of Christ means having the Father and the Son.
The practical rule: do not take such a teacher into the house.

outline.title: Joy at children walking in truth
Love one another, and keep the commandments

people.name: The elder
people.note: The writer, who gives no other name.

people.name: The elect lady and her children
people.note: The addressee: a woman, or a church pictured as a lady. Her “elect sister” sends greetings.

places.name: Ephesus
places.note: Not named in the letter. Plummer, Westcott and Easton think it was written from the same place as 1 John.

author.text: Again “the elder”, with the same opening and closing formulas as 2 John. Who the elder was is discussed below.

recipients.text: “The wellbeloved Gaius”, who walks in the truth and has welcomed travelling believers. The name was very common; Plummer thinks a link with any other Gaius of the New Testament is “possible, but nothing more”, and Law calls such identifications fanciful.

writtenFrom.text: Probably Ephesus, like 1 and 2 John, by the same tradition.

date.text: Disputed with 1 John; placed after the first letter and close in time to 2 John. Brooke notes that the shared phrasing of 2 and 3 John points to common authorship and nearness of date.

occasion.text: Missionaries who went out “for his name's sake” had been welcomed by Gaius. Diotrephes, a local leader, refused them, spoke against the elder, and put out of the church those who would receive them. The elder praises Gaius, vouches for Demetrius, and plans to come in person. This is the reading of Law, Brooke and Plummer.

themes.text: Walking in the truth: “I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth.”
Hospitality as partnership: those who help travelling teachers are “fellowhelpers to the truth”.
Follow the good, not the evil: “He that doeth good is of God.”
Testimony. The words for witness and bearing witness come five times in fourteen verses.
The writer's “true witness” formula, “ye know that our record is true”, echoes John's Gospel (19:35; 21:24); Westcott lists it as a Johannine trait.

Is “I wrote unto the church” a reference to 2 John? Zahn, Schmiedel and Findlay thought so; Harnack, Brooke and Law did not, since 2 John deals with false teachers and 3 John with a domineering official. (As reported by Law.)
Two sides of one picture: Plummer, quoting Bishop Alexander, says 2 John condemns “the spirit of heresy” and 3 John “the spirit of schism”.
Verse numbering differs. The King James has 14 verses; Tischendorf's text, like many modern editions, makes the closing “Peace be to thee…” a 15th.
A slow road into the canon, shared with 2 John: Eusebius counted it among the disputed books, and the Syriac Peshitta does not include it.

keyVerses.why: The elder's wish for Gaius: to prosper and be in health.
“No greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth.”
Receiving travelling teachers makes one a fellow-worker for the truth.
“He that doeth good is of God.”

words.note: Counted in the sense “know” only; the King James tags show 3 because of “shall see” in verse 14.

people.name: Gaius
people.note: The recipient, a generous host to travelling teachers: “wellbeloved”, he “walkest in the truth” and “doest faithfully”. Other men called Gaius appear in Acts 19:29, Acts 20:4, Romans 16:23 and 1 Corinthians 1:14, but the name was common and no link is certain. The Apostolic Constitutions list a Gaius as an early bishop of Pergamum; Plummer says he may be this Gaius.

people.name: Diotrephes
people.note: A local leader who “loveth to have the preeminence” (one Greek word, philoprōteuōn, found nowhere else in the New Testament). He refused the elder's people, spoke against him “with malicious words”, and cast out of the church those who welcomed them. His name means “nourished by Jove”. Law sees no hint of false doctrine, only pride of place; Easton calls him a Judaizer. He is named nowhere else in the Bible.

people.name: Demetrius
people.note: Commended: he “hath good report of all men, and of the truth itself”. Law, Plummer and Brooke think he probably carried the letter or led the travelling missionaries. Smith thinks it very doubtful that he is the silversmith of Ephesus (Acts 19:24). The Apostolic Constitutions name a Demetrius as an early bishop of Philadelphia.

people.name: The elder
people.note: The writer, who has written to the church and plans to come and “speak face to face”.

people.name: The brethren and strangers
people.note: Travelling missionaries who “went forth” for the name of Christ, “taking nothing of the Gentiles”.

places.name: Ephesus
places.note: Not named in the letter. Tradition places the elder's letters at Ephesus.

views.label: The apostle John wrote all three
views.holders: Irenaeus (c. 180); Dionysius of Alexandria for 1 John (c. 250s); B. F. Westcott; A. Plummer; Robert Law; William Smith; M. G. Easton

argument.text: Irenaeus quotes 1 and 2 John as the work of “John, the disciple of the Lord”. Westcott argues that “the elder” marks a unique standing and fits the aged apostle, and Law notes that an apostle could call himself an elder, as Peter does. Plummer holds that the case for 2 John carries 3 John with it.

views.label: The apostle wrote 1 John; John the Elder wrote 2 and 3 John
views.holders: “Many” in Jerome's day (392); raised as an open question by Eusebius (c. 325); A. E. Brooke (1912)

argument.text: Papias, as quoted by Eusebius, names two Johns: the apostle, and “the presbyter John”, a disciple of the Lord. Eusebius adds the report of two tombs at Ephesus, each called John's. Jerome says many held the last two letters to be the presbyter's. Brooke finds this best supported by tradition and by the letters themselves, while leaving the Elder's relation to the apostle an unsolved mystery.

views.label: Different hands, or none of them the apostle's
views.holders: Joseph Scaliger (1540–1609); F. C. Baur, H. J. Holtzmann, Pfleiderer and von Soden, as reported by Robert Law (1915)

argument.text: Scaliger rejected all three letters as not the apostle's. Baur and others argued that the Gospel and 1 John had different authors, Baur explaining the likeness as imitation; Jülicher, Wrede and Wernle, by contrast, accepted a single author.

questions.question: Who is “the elect lady” of 2 John?

views.label: A woman named Electa
views.holders: Clement of Alexandria (c. 200); Robert Law (1915), who prefers “the lady Electa” or “my dear lady Eklekte”

argument.text: Clement says the letter was written to a lady “by name Electa”, and the tone is personal. Against it, Plummer and Brooke point to verse 13: her sister would then bear the same very unusual name.

views.label: A woman named Kyria
views.holders: Mentioned as possible by William Smith, M. G. Easton and A. E. Brooke

argument.text: Kyria, “lady”, is known as a woman's name. Against it, Plummer thinks John would then have written “to Kyria, the elect”, as he writes “to Gaius, the beloved”.

views.label: A real Christian woman, not named
views.holders: A. Plummer; William Smith; M. G. Easton

argument.text: Its twin, 3 John, is plainly written to one person, and a sustained allegory seems unlikely in so slight a letter; Plummer compares Philemon.

views.label: A church, pictured as a lady
views.holders: A. E. Brooke; Davidson (quoted by Plummer); Jülicher (as cited by Brooke)

argument.text: The greeting from “all they that have known the truth” suits a community; the address moves between “thee” and “you”; the contents are not private in character. The “elect sister” would then be a sister church.

views.label: Undecided
views.holders: B. F. Westcott; Robert Law

argument.text: Westcott finds no solution satisfactory, and Law notes the question has been debated since ancient times and remains unsolved.

views.label: The last decade of the first century
views.holders: B. F. Westcott

argument.text: The state of the church, and false teaching that matches Cerinthus in Asia at the end of the century.

views.label: About AD 85–95
views.holders: A. Plummer

argument.text: A long gap after Revelation, the tone of an old man, and a clear stand against Gnosticism.

views.label: The close of the first century
views.holders: William Smith

argument.text: Smith gives the date without reasons.

views.label: No later than about AD 110
views.holders: A. E. Brooke

argument.text: Papias and Polycarp already knew 1 John, so it cannot be later than the first decade of the second century.

views.label: Before AD 70
views.holders: An older reading with no holder named in the sources consulted; recorded and rejected by Plummer

argument.text: It took “it is the last time” to mean the eve of Jerusalem's fall. Plummer answers that Jerusalem had fallen at least a dozen years before the probable date.

views.label: 2 and 3 John soon after 1 John, from the same place
views.holders: A. Plummer; B. F. Westcott; M. G. Easton

argument.text: The short letters share formulas with each other and take 1 John's teaching for granted.

questions.question: Who were the opponents the letters warn against?

views.label: Cerinthus, or teaching like his
views.holders: The tradition from Irenaeus onward; B. F. Westcott; A. E. Brooke (for chapter 5, “the most probable view”); Robert Law

argument.text: Irenaeus reports that Cerinthus taught that “Christ descended upon him in the form of a dove” at Jesus' baptism and departed before the cross. That would be a Christ who came “by water” only, which 1 John 5:6 denies: “not by water only, but by water and blood”. Irenaeus also tells, from Polycarp, of John fleeing a bath-house at Ephesus because Cerinthus was inside, and says John's Gospel was written against his error; later writers applied this to the letters.

views.label: Docetism, with carelessness about sin
views.holders: Robert Law

argument.text: Docetism held that Christ only seemed to have a body; Ignatius, about 110, wrote against those who said “He only seemed to suffer”, and Polycarp echoes 1 John 4:3. Law thinks the same opponents probably also held that what the body does does not matter morally, which would explain the letter's claims about sin.

views.label: A Jewish strand among the opponents
views.holders: A. E. Brooke, who allows for it

argument.text: The denial that “Jesus is the Christ” could come from Jewish opponents.

views.label: Several errors, not one party
views.holders: A. E. Brooke

argument.text: “Many antichrists” and “many false prophets”: truth is one, but error takes many forms.

views.label: No single heresy is the main target
views.holders: B. F. Westcott

argument.text: John writes to welcome what he knows to be the Gospel, rather than to overthrow one particular false opinion.

questions.question: Are “the three that bear record in heaven” (1 John 5:7–8) part of what John wrote?

views.label: Not part of the original letter
views.holders: B. F. Westcott; F. H. A. Scrivener; A. Plummer; A. E. Brooke, and 19th-century textual critics generally

argument.text: The King James reads: “there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one. And there are three that bear witness in earth…”. These critics report that the words from “in heaven” to “in earth” are missing from every Greek uncial and from all but a handful of very late Greek copies, and from the Syriac, Coptic, Ethiopic, Arabic and Armenian translations and the oldest Latin. They first appear as part of the letter in Latin writers from Priscillian (died 385) onward. Erasmus left them out of his Greek editions of 1516 and 1519 and put them in the third (1522), from which they passed into English Bibles until the Revised Version of 1881. Of the site's three Greek texts, only the Textus Receptus behind the King James contains them. Westcott calls them a gloss added “without any signs of bad faith”; Brooke says they break the passage's natural sequence.

views.label: Genuine
views.holders: John Gill (1746–48), and a minority of earlier writers

argument.text: Gill argued that the words stand in many early Latin manuscripts, that the prologue to the letters bearing Jerome's name complains of their omission, that nine of Robert Stephens's sixteen copies had them, and that early writers cite them; the critics above answer each point.

claim.text: Echoes 1 John 4:3: whoever does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is antichrist.

canon.label: Papias
canon.who: Papias, as quoted by Eusebius (early 2nd century)

claim.text: Eusebius says Papias used testimonies from “the first Epistle of John”.
Quotes 1 John 2:18–22 and 2 John 7–8 as written by John, the disciple of the Lord.

Quotes 1 John's opening freely, and says that two letters of John are held in the catholic church. The Latin is corrupt, and which two letters are meant is unclear; Brooke notes evidence of a period when 1 and 2 John were accepted without the third.
Calls 1 John the “larger Epistle”, and comments on 2 John.
Accepts 1 John, “an epistle of very few lines”, and perhaps a second and third, “but not all consider them genuine”.

canon.label: Dionysius of Alexandria
canon.who: Dionysius of Alexandria, as quoted by Eusebius (c. 250s)

claim.text: Holds that the Gospel and 1 John share one author, and notes that the “reputed” second and third letters bear not the name John but “the elder”.
1 John is accepted without dispute; 2 and 3 John are among the disputed books, whether by the evangelist or by another of the same name.
Gives 1 John to the apostle and reports that many held the other two to be the work of John the presbyter.

parallels.title: 1 John and the Gospel of John

pairs.note: The opening: the Word, the beginning, seen and witnessed (John 1:1–2, 14). Dionysius; Westcott.
Seeing and bearing witness. Westcott.
“That your joy may be full” (also John 16:24). Westcott; Law.
Light, and walking in it rather than in darkness. Law.
Paraklētos, “advocate” or “Comforter”: only here and in John 14:16, 14:26, 15:26 and 16:7. Law.
The new commandment to love one another (also 1 John 3:23; John 15:12). Westcott; Law.
“The true light”. Law.
Walking in darkness, not knowing where one goes: near-identical wording. Westcott; Brooke.
God's word abiding in you. Westcott.
Abiding for ever. Westcott; Law.
Called, or made, the sons of God. Law; Brooke.
Christ without sin. Westcott.
The devil, a murderer “from the beginning” (1 John 3:8, 12, 15). Westcott; Law.
“If the world hate you”: identical clause. Westcott.
Passed “from death unto life”: identical phrase. Westcott; Law.
Laying down one's life (also John 15:13). Westcott; Law.
Doing what pleases God. Westcott.
The Spirit of truth (also John 15:26, 16:13), and hearing God (John 8:47). Westcott; Brooke.
God's only begotten Son, sent in love (also John 1:14, 18). Brooke; Law.
“No man hath seen God at any time”: identical in the King James. Law; Brooke.
Mutual indwelling, and knowing and believing (also John 6:69, 15:10). Westcott.
Overcoming the world. Westcott; Law.
Water and blood, with an eyewitness who bears record. Law.
A greater witness. Westcott.
The two statements of purpose: believing, and life through his name. Westcott.
Knowing the true God is eternal life. Westcott; Brooke.

claim.text: Twenty-six places where 1 John and John's Gospel share wording or ideas, each named by Westcott, Law, Brooke or Dionysius of Alexandria. Dionysius already observed in the third century that “the Gospel and Epistle agree with each other and begin in the same manner”; Westcott calls the two openings complementary rather than parallel. Pairs marked “wording” share a phrase or a rare word; the rest share an idea.

pairs.note: Not a new commandment, but the one “from the beginning”.
“That we love one another.”
Love is keeping his commandments.
Confessing that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh.
Antichrist.
The deceiver and antichrist.
Having the Father through the Son; abiding in what was heard.
“That our joy may be full.”

claim.text: 2 John repeats 1 John's teaching almost line for line. Law calls it in effect a summary of the first letter.

pairs.note: “The elder unto … whom I love in the truth.”
“I rejoiced greatly”: a Greek phrase found nowhere else in the New Testament, says Law.
Children walking in truth.
Much to write, but not with paper and ink, or ink and pen.
Hoping to “speak face to face”.

claim.text: The two short letters open and close in the same words. Brooke sets them side by side and says the likeness points to one author writing at about the same time. They are almost exactly the same length, which Brooke thinks was probably set by the size of an ordinary papyrus sheet.

timelines.title: How “the three heavenly witnesses” entered the printed Bible

events.label: Cyprian (died 258) writes “and the three are one”. Most critics read this as verse 8 applied to the Trinity; Scrivener thinks Cyprian read verse 7 in his Latin copies.
Priscillian (died 385) is the first to quote the words as part of 1 John, in a variant form.
African writers quote it: the confession of 484 recorded by Victor of Vita, then Vigilius of Thapsus and Fulgentius.
The Greek acts of the Fourth Lateran Council contain the clause.
Greek manuscript 162, 15th century: one of the very few Greek copies to have it.
Erasmus's first Greek New Testament leaves it out.
Erasmus's second edition leaves it out.
Erasmus's third edition puts it in, on the authority of Codex Montfortianus.
The King James Version includes it.
John Gill defends the words as genuine.
The Revised Version leaves it out.
Westcott, Plummer, Scrivener and Brooke conclude the words entered from a Latin note.

claim.text: The King James Version, following the printed Greek text of its day, includes these words. Nearly all Greek manuscripts and the oldest translations do not have them, and 19th-century textual critics such as Westcott, Scrivener, Plummer and Brooke concluded they entered from a Latin note. A minority of earlier writers, such as John Gill, defended them. Dates are as these critics report them.

maps.title: Ephesus and the churches of Asia, by tradition

stops.name: Ephesus
stops.note: Irenaeus says John lived here until the time of Trajan; Eusebius reports two tombs here, each called John's.

stops.name: Pergamum
stops.note: The Apostolic Constitutions list a Gaius as an early bishop here; Plummer says he may be the Gaius of 3 John.

stops.name: Philadelphia
stops.note: The Apostolic Constitutions list a Demetrius, ordained by John, as an early bishop here.

claim.text: None of the three letters names a place. Early tradition sets John at Ephesus late in his life, and the letters are usually linked with the churches of the province of Asia around it.

edges.label: receives and sends on their way
bear witness of his love before the church
forbids them, and casts them out

claim.text: The whole story of 3 John in one picture: a host, a blocker and a newcomer. The edges use the letter's own words; the reading of the story follows Law, Brooke and Plummer.

flows.title: The Old Testament behind John's letters

claim.text: John's three letters quote no Old Testament passage. The one band is 1 John's single clear allusion: Cain, who “slew his brother” (Genesis 4:8), set against love that lays down its life. 2 John and 3 John draw on no Old Testament passage at all.
